title: From a Base to Wider Influence
imageAlt: A conceptual chain connects a governing base, supplies and communications with particular places. It does not shade every island as controlled.
content:
You have compared Cebu and Manila as colonial bases. Now ask how officials tried to extend authority beyond a base. Issuing an order was only one step. People had to carry messages, obtain supplies and make decisions in the places affected. Existing trade connections and local relationships mattered.

The Library of Congress discussion of early colonial history describes the importance of regional merchants and local interests. These connections could support a continuing Spanish presence, but did not make every community accept it. A base was a starting point for attempts to expand authority, not proof of success everywhere.

Read the link diagram as a thinking guide. For each arrow, ask what action and whose work connected the places. It is not an exact route map or a complete account of expansion.
clues: A base
Officials could issue decisions from a colonial base, but needed connections to act elsewhere.
People maintained links
Merchants and local participants helped sustain regional connections. Geography alone did not carry messages or supplies.
Check the result
A connection or an order is not proof of effective authority in every place.
task: Which explanation connects a base with attempts to expand authority?
Messages, supplies and relationships were needed to act beyond the base
A base automatically governed every island
Geography alone carried every order
One official performed all regional tasks
reason: Bases needed people, supplies and connections. The reach of authority must be investigated in particular places.
definition: A link through which people, goods or information can move.

title: Pressure Is Different from Agreement
imageAlt: Three teaching cards distinguish a request, a threat and evidence of a response. They are fictional examples, not original speeches.
content:
Expansion could involve force and pressure as well as agreements. Coercion means trying to make someone obey through threats or force. An official might describe an action as peaceful even when affected people faced serious pressure. Read the action and its setting, not just a favorable label.

The Cebu and Mactan lessons supplied named examples of demands and conflict. Use them as background, without assuming every later place followed the same sequence. Explaining how coercion worked is different from approving it. We do not earn points for harm in this investigation.

Try a fictional comparison. One card records a request; another adds a threat if it is refused. Ask what changed. A reply under pressure cannot automatically be treated as evidence that every person freely welcomed outside rule. The cards help you reason; they do not quote historical participants.
clues: Identify the action
A threat or use of force is different from a request without a threat.
Check the setting
A recorded agreement should be considered alongside pressure or conflict surrounding it.
Keep the limit
One agreement does not reveal every resident's wishes or justify coercion.
task: A fictional official threatens punishment unless people agree. What should a report identify?
Coercion, rather than assume a freely welcomed agreement
Proof that every person freely wanted the demand
Evidence that no pressure existed
A reason to ignore the affected people
reason: Identify pressure and force in context. An agreement under pressure is not proof of universal, freely given consent.
definition: Trying to make someone obey by using force or threats.

title: Communities Made Different Choices
imageAlt: A comparison guide separates negotiation, adaptation and resistance. These are possible actions, not permanent labels for whole peoples.
content:
People responded to colonial demands in different ways. Negotiation means discussing terms. Adaptation means changing some practices in response to circumstances. Resistance means opposing a demand or an attempt to impose authority. These are actions to investigate, not permanent labels for whole peoples.

A community could negotiate at one time and resist a different demand later. People within a place could also have different interests. Do not assume one leader's action reveals every person's thoughts. Your earlier Cebu agreement and Manila Bay resistance examples show why separate settings need separate evidence.

For this fictional report task, compare two records: discussion about supplies and refusal of a later demand. The records do not have to contradict each other. Ask who acted, when, and in response to what. Avoid treating adaptation as proof of approval of every part of colonial rule.
clues: Negotiation
Discussion of terms can address a particular issue rather than all future demands.
Adaptation
Changing a practice does not establish approval of everything an outside authority does.
Resistance
Opposing a demand can occur alongside other forms of contact. Responses can change over time.
task: Which report treats different responses carefully?
Identify who acted, when and toward which demand, allowing choices to change
Give every resident one permanent response
Treat adaptation as consent to all future demands
Assume discussion and later refusal cannot both happen
reason: Negotiation, adaptation and resistance depend on people, issues and time. One action is not a permanent label for everyone.
definition: An action people take toward events or demands affecting them.

title: Why Reach Varied
imageAlt: A reach checklist asks about communications, resources and local authority. It is not a historical boundary map or a claim that terrain determines culture.
content:
A claim of authority can be wider than its practical reach. To check effective control, investigate whether decisions were carried out and what people did in response. A colored area on a modern teaching map cannot answer all those questions.

Travel conditions and supplies affected contact, but terrain alone did not decide history. Local organization, knowledge, alliances and resistance mattered too. Avoid calling a community backward because it maintained its own leadership. Different relationships with colonial institutions do not rank people's worth.

Work through a fictional case: an order is issued, but the record gives no evidence of its delivery or enforcement in another place. You may report that an order was issued. You need more evidence to claim it was followed there. Keep time and place attached to your conclusion, because authority could expand, weaken or be contested.
clues: A claim
An official's statement of authority is not the same as evidence of its effect.
Several factors
Communications, resources and local political decisions could shape the reach of an institution.
A careful conclusion
Ask where and when a decision was carried out. Do not infer universal control from one order.
task: An order exists, but no record shows enforcement in a distant community. What conclusion fits?
The order was issued; its effect there still needs evidence
Every resident there necessarily obeyed
Terrain proves the community had no organization
The order reveals every person's motive
reason: Effective reach needs evidence of actions in particular places and times. A claim, map color or terrain feature alone is insufficient.
definition: Authority actually exercised in practice, rather than only claimed.

title: Evidence of Continuing Local Authority
imageAlt: Two later examples distinguish Ifugao resistance and Sulu diplomacy. Their different places and periods do not represent one identical response by all communities.
content:
Did colonial claims erase every form of local authority? Named examples help test that idea. National Museum material describing research in Ifugao explains resistance to Spanish conquest. This is an example of local organization and agency, not proof that every highland community had an identical history.

NCCA's history of Muslim communities discusses diplomacy and conflict involving the Sulu sultanate and Spanish officials, including a treaty in 1726. This later example shows why we must keep periods distinct. It is not an event from Legazpi's 1565 expedition. Diplomacy does not by itself prove that all parties understood terms identically or that conflict never occurred.

Compare the examples without turning Ifugao or Sulu into timeless, uniform groups. Both help question universal-control claims, but they involve different settings. Chapter 11 will develop these histories; this mission introduces the evidence question rather than covering them completely.
clues: An Ifugao example
National Museum research material describes resistance to Spanish conquest. Do not apply one example to every highland community.
A later Sulu example
NCCA discusses Sulu diplomacy, conflict and a 1726 treaty. This is later than the 1565 expedition.
Separate contexts
Two distinct examples challenge a claim of uniform control without proving that every community had the same experience.
task: Which comparison uses these examples responsibly?
Keep Ifugao resistance and later Sulu diplomacy in their own settings when testing universal-control claims
Put the 1726 treaty into Legazpi's 1565 voyage
Treat every highland and Muslim community as identical
Assume diplomacy proves no conflict ever happened
reason: Ifugao resistance and later Sulu diplomacy belong to distinct contexts. They help question uniform-control claims without erasing differences.
definition: The ability of a community to make and maintain its own decisions.

title: Explain Expansion Without Erasing People
imageAlt: A report checklist connects an attempt to expand authority, a local response and evidence of actual reach. The chapter remains unfinished.
content:
Build an explanation rather than color an entire archipelago as controlled. Start with a base and the connections needed to act beyond it. Identify whether the evidence describes a request, pressure, an agreement or force. Name a local response and keep the issue, place and time attached.

Then check the result. An order is evidence of a decision being issued, not automatically of its enforcement everywhere. Different communities and different periods need their own evidence. The Ifugao and Sulu examples introduce distinct histories; neither supplies one response for all people.

Use this fictional report frame: Officials attempted [action]. At [place and time], people responded by [supported action]. The evidence shows [effect], but does not establish [unsupported claim]. This is a classroom guide, not an original speech.

Use the mission quiz to check what you learned. If a topic is difficult, revisit its lesson and try targeted practice before another quiz attempt. Passing earns the mission reward once. Complete all missions, then pass the chapter challenge to earn the chapter badge.
clues: Connect the attempt
Identify the action and the links or resources it needed.
Include people
Distinguish coercion, negotiation, adaptation and resistance in their own contexts.
State the limit
Keep official claims separate from effective reach and preserve differences across places and periods.
task: Which final explanation best connects the investigation?
Expansion depended on connections, pressure and local responses, and its actual reach varied
One colonial order proves identical control everywhere
All communities made one permanent choice
Later examples can be moved to 1565 without changing their meaning
reason: Explain attempts, local actions and actual effects using place-specific and time-specific evidence.
definition: An account linking events and evidence while stating limits and uncertainty.
